claim: TORC2-dependent protein kinase Ypk1 phosphorylates ceramide synthase to stimulate synthesis of complex sphingolipids.
source: TORC2-dependent protein kinase Ypk1 phosphorylates ceramide synthase to stimulate synthesis of complex sphingolipids
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with multiple experimental approaches including in vitro kinase assays, phospho-site mapping, and sphingolipidomics.

claim: Ypk1 alleviates negative regulation of L-serine:palmitoyl-CoA acyltransferase, upregulating production of long-chain base precursors to sphingolipids.
source: Ypk1, among other actions, alleviates negative regulation of L-serine:palmitoyl-CoA acyltransferase, upregulating production of long-chain base precursors to sphingolipids.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Roelants et al., 2011; Berchtold et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012) showing Ypk1 phosphorylates Orm proteins to relieve SPT inhibition.

claim: A three-tiered genome-wide screen identified both catalytic subunits of the ceramide synthase complex as Ypk1 substrates.
source: To explore other roles for TORC2-Ypk1 signaling in membrane homeostasis, we devised a three-tiered genome-wide screen to identify additional Ypk1 substrates, which pinpointed both catalytic subunits of the ceramide synthase complex.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and execution of a bioinformatic, genetic (SDL), and biochemical screening approach that identified Lac1 and Lag1.

claim: Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of ceramide synthase subunits increased upon either sphingolipid depletion or heat shock.
source: Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of both proteins increased upon either sphingolipid depletion or heat shock and was important for cell survival.
evidence: Demonstrated by Phos-tag gel analysis showing increased phosphorylation of Lac1 and Lag1 after myriocin, aureobasidin A treatment, or heat shock (Figures 3B, 4A, 4B).

claim: Phosphorylation of ceramide synthase by Ypk1 was important for cell survival under sphingolipid stress.
source: Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of both proteins increased upon either sphingolipid depletion or heat shock and was important for cell survival.
evidence: Cells expressing non-phosphorylatable Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) showed reduced growth on myriocin and aureobasidin A compared to wild-type or phosphomimetic mutants (Figure 4C).

claim: Phosphorylation of ceramide synthase increased its specific activity.
source: Sphingolipidomics, other biochemical measurements and genetic analysis demonstrated that these modifications of ceramide synthase increased its specific activity and stimulated channeling of long-chain base precursors into sphingolipid end-products.
evidence: In vitro ceramide synthase assays showed that Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) phosphomimetic mutant had approximately 2-fold higher specific activity than wild-type or non-phosphorylatable mutants (Figure 6C).

claim: Phosphorylation of ceramide synthase stimulated channeling of long-chain base precursors into sphingolipid end-products.
source: Sphingolipidomics, other biochemical measurements and genetic analysis demonstrated that these modifications of ceramide synthase increased its specific activity and stimulated channeling of long-chain base precursors into sphingolipid end-products.
evidence: LC-MS analysis showed that non-phosphorylatable mutants accumulated more LCBs and LCBPs, while phosphomimetic mutants had lower levels (Figure 6A). Pulse-labeling showed phosphomimetic mutants produced more complex sphingolipids (Figure 6B).

claim: Control of ceramide synthase by Ypk1 prevents accumulation of intermediates that could compromise cell growth by stimulating autophagy.
source: Control at this branch point also prevents accumulation of intermediates that could compromise cell growth by stimulating autophagy.
evidence: Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells expressing constitutively active Ypk1 showed increased GFP-Atg8 processing (autophagy marker) and accumulated LCBPs. Deletion of ATG1 partially rescued the growth defect (Figures 7E, 7F).

claim: TORC2 stimulates Ypk1 and Ypk2 function by phosphorylating at least two C-terminal sites under membrane stress conditions.
source: Under such conditions of membrane stress, TORC2 stimulates Ypk1 and Ypk2 function by phosphorylating at least two C-terminal sites (Kamada et al., 2005; Roelants et al., 2011; Niles et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work demonstrating TORC2-dependent phosphorylation of Ypk1/Ypk2 C-terminal sites.

claim: Constitutively-active Ypk1 and Ypk2 alleles bypass the need for functional TORC2.
source: Constitutively-active Ypk1 and Ypk2 alleles bypass the need for functional TORC2, indicating that Ypk1 and Ypk2 are solely responsible for executing all the essential downstream functions of TORC2 (Kamada et al., 2005; Roelants et al., 2011; Niles et al., 2012).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by citations to previous studies showing that constitutively active Ypk1/Ypk2 can rescue TORC2 deficiency.

claim: Ypk1 phosphorylates and negatively regulates Fpk1, a protein kinase responsible for activation of PM-localized aminophospholipid flippases.
source: Ypk1 phosphorylates and negatively regulates Fpk1, a protein kinase responsible for activation of PM-localized aminophospholipid flippases (Roelants et al., 2010), thereby fine-tuning the phosphatidylethanolamine content of the inner leaflet of the PM bilayer.
evidence: This is stated as a known Ypk1 target with citation to previous work (Roelants et al., 2010).

claim: Ypk1 phosphorylates and alleviates the inhibitory function of Orm1 and Orm2 that impede SPT function.
source: Ypk1 also phosphorylates and alleviates the inhibitory function of two endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized proteins (Orm1 and Orm2) that impede the function of the first enzyme unique to sphingolipid biosynthesis, L-serine:palmitoyl-CoA acyltransferase (SPT) (Roelants et al., 2011; Berchtold et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012), thereby increasing the rate of formation of the long-chain base precursor (phytosphingosine) to yeast sphingolipids.
evidence: This is stated as a known function of Ypk1 with citations to multiple previous studies (Roelants et al., 2011; Berchtold et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012).

claim: Ypk1 phosphorylates and inhibits Gpd1, a primary source of glycerol-3P for production of glycerophospholipids.
source: Ypk1 also phosphorylates and inhibits one of the two isoforms (Gpd1) of glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, a primary source of glycerol-3P for production of glycerophospholipids (Lee et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is stated as a known Ypk1 target with citation to previous work (Lee et al., 2012b).

claim: In response to hyperosmotic shock, TORC2 activity is markedly decreased, preventing Ypk1-mediated inhibition of Gpd1.
source: In response to hyperosmotic shock, and in contrast to other PM stressors, TORC2 activity is markedly decreased, preventing Ypk1-mediated inhibition of Gpd1 [which also gets upregulated transcriptionally (Ansell et al., 1997)], thereby greatly increasing synthesis of glycerol-3P, which is dephosphorylated to produce glycerol, an innocuous osmolyte that yeast cells accumulate as a means to counteract the increase in external osmotic pressure (Lee et al., 2012b).
evidence: This mechanism is described with citations to previous work (Ansell et al., 1997; Lee et al., 2012b).

claim: The bioinformatic approach identified three known Ypk1 substrates (Fpk1, Orm1 and Orm2).
source: Reassuringly, our approach identified three known Ypk1 substrates (Fpk1, Orm1 and Orm2); absence of Fpk2 and Gpd1 from the list generated solely by the MOTIPS search criteria arose from the fact that these substrates contain only a single predicted site that is not presently recorded in PhosphoGRID.
evidence: This validates the bioinformatic screening approach by showing it can identify known substrates.

claim: Lac1 and Lag1 are apparent paralogs with 69% identity and 77% similarity at the primary sequence level.
source: Lac1 (418 residues) and Lag1 (411 residues) are apparent paralogs at the primary sequence level (69% identity, 77% similarity) (Byrne and Wolfe, 2005) and are polytopic integral proteins in the ER membrane with the predicted Ypk1 site in each protein residing near its N-terminus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Byrne and Wolfe, 2005) analyzing sequence relationships.

claim: The N-termini of Lac1 and Lag1 are exposed to the cytosol.
source: It has been shown that the N-termini of these proteins are exposed to the cytosol (Kageyama-Yahara and Riezman, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Kageyama-Yahara and Riezman, 2006) determining membrane topology.

claim: Lac1 and Lag1, along with Lip1, are demonstrated constituents of the ceramide synthase complex.
source: Along with a small accessory subunit Lip1 (150 residues), Lac1 and Lag1 are demonstrated constituents of the ceramide synthase complex (Schorling et al., 2001; Vallée and Riezman, 2005), which catalyzes N-acylation of the free amino group on the long-chain base (LCB), mainly phytosphingosine in yeast, using fatty acyl-CoA as the acyl donor, thereby forming phytoceramide (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Schorling et al., 2001; Vallée and Riezman, 2005) characterizing the ceramide synthase complex.

claim: The ceramide synthase complex catalyzes N-acylation of long-chain bases using fatty acyl-CoA as the acyl donor to form phytoceramide.
source: Along with a small accessory subunit Lip1 (150 residues), Lac1 and Lag1 are demonstrated constituents of the ceramide synthase complex (Schorling et al., 2001; Vallée and Riezman, 2005), which catalyzes N-acylation of the free amino group on the long-chain base (LCB), mainly phytosphingosine in yeast, using fatty acyl-CoA as the acyl donor, thereby forming phytoceramide (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the enzymatic reaction catalyzed by ceramide synthase, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: lac1Δ or lag1Δ single mutants are viable, whereas a lac1Δ lag1Δ double mutant is either inviable or extremely slow growing.
source: Genetically, Lac1 and Lag1 appear to play overlapping functional roles; lac1Δ or lag1Δ single mutants are viable, whereas a lac1Δ lag1Δ double mutant is reportedly either inviable (Jiang et al., 1998) or extremely slow growing (Barz and Walter, 1999; Schorling et al., 2001; Vallée and Riezman, 2005).
evidence: This genetic relationship is stated with citations to multiple previous studies (Jiang et al., 1998; Barz and Walter, 1999; Schorling et al., 2001; Vallée and Riezman, 2005).

claim: The ceramide synthase reaction lies at an important branch point in the sphingolipid metabolic network.
source: The ceramide synthase reaction lies at an important branch point in the sphingolipid metabolic network (Figure 2B) because de novo synthesis of ceramides both consumes LCBs and prevents conversion of LCBs to their 1-phosphorylated derivatives (LCBPs).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2B showing the pathway branch point.

claim: The rate of ceramide synthesis is tightly coupled to the levels of both LCBs and LCBPs.
source: Thus, the rate of ceramide synthesis is tightly coupled to the levels of both LCBs and LCBPs (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003); and, moreover, the balance between ceramides and total LCBs and LCBPs affects growth rate in both fungi (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003) and mammalian cells (Spiegel and Milstien, 2003).
evidence: This metabolic relationship is stated with citations to previous work (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003; Spiegel and Milstien, 2003).

claim: The balance between ceramides and total LCBs and LCBPs affects growth rate in both fungi and mammalian cells.
source: Thus, the rate of ceramide synthesis is tightly coupled to the levels of both LCBs and LCBPs (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003); and, moreover, the balance between ceramides and total LCBs and LCBPs affects growth rate in both fungi (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003) and mammalian cells (Spiegel and Milstien, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work in fungi (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003) and mammalian cells (Spiegel and Milstien, 2003).

claim: Both Lac1 and Lag1 displayed a readily detectable SDL phenotype.
source: Among the bioinformatically predicted substrates, both Lac1 and Lag1 displayed a readily detectable SDL phenotype (Figure 2C) and both GST-Lac1(1–76) and GST-Lag1(1–80) served as in vitro substrates for Ypk1, albeit with the phosphorylation of Lac1 being reproducibly much more robust than Lag1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing growth defects upon overexpression in ypk1-as ypk2Δ cells with inhibitor.

claim: GST-Lac1(1–76) and GST-Lag1(1–80) served as in vitro substrates for Ypk1.
source: Among the bioinformatically predicted substrates, both Lac1 and Lag1 displayed a readily detectable SDL phenotype (Figure 2C) and both GST-Lac1(1–76) and GST-Lag1(1–80) served as in vitro substrates for Ypk1, albeit with the phosphorylation of Lac1 being reproducibly much more robust than Lag1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D showing 32P incorporation into GST-Lac1 and GST-Lag1 in kinase assays with purified Ypk1.

claim: Phosphorylation of Lac1 by Ypk1 is reproducibly much more robust than phosphorylation of Lag1.
source: Among the bioinformatically predicted substrates, both Lac1 and Lag1 displayed a readily detectable SDL phenotype (Figure 2C) and both GST-Lac1(1–76) and GST-Lag1(1–80) served as in vitro substrates for Ypk1, albeit with the phosphorylation of Lac1 being reproducibly much more robust than Lag1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2D showing stronger 32P incorporation into Lac1 compared to Lag1 in in vitro kinase assays.

claim: Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation of Lac1 and Lag1 occurred exclusively at Ser23 and Ser24.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis confirmed that the Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation of both substrates occurred exclusively at the predicted phospho-acceptor site(s), specifically Ser23 and Ser24 in both proteins (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D showing that S23A S24A mutations abolish Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation in vitro.

claim: Both Lac1 and Lag1 migrated as two species on Phos-tag gels, with the slower species representing phosphorylation at S23 and S24.
source: Both Lac1 (Figure 3A, left) and Lag1 (Figure 3A, right) migrated as two species, and the slower of the two could be attributed to phosphorylation because it was eliminated if the sample was pre-treated with calf intestinal phosphatase. This slower mobility species represented phosphorylation at S23 and S24 because the band was also eliminated in Lac1(S23A S24A) and Lag1(S23A S24A) mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A showing Phos-tag gel analysis with phosphatase treatment and S23A S24A mutants.

claim: The majority of Lac1 was present in the cell as the phosphorylated isoform, whereas the opposite was true for Lag1.
source: In agreement with their relative efficacies as in vitro substrates (Figure 2D), we found that, reproducibly, the majority of Lac1 was present in the cell as the slower mobility isoform, whereas the opposite was true for Lag1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3A showing the relative intensities of phosphorylated vs unphosphorylated bands for Lac1 and Lag1 on Phos-tag gels.

claim: Absence of Ypk1 totally abrogated the appearance of phosphorylated Lac1 and Lag1.
source: As observed previously for two other bona fide substrates, Orm1 and Orm2 (Roelants et al., 2011), absence of Ypk1 totally abrogated the appearance of phosphorylated Lac1 (Figure 3B) and phosphorylated Lag1 (data not shown), whereas elimination of Ypk2 had no effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing loss of the phosphorylated band in ypk1Δ but not ypk2Δ cells.

claim: Ypk1 is the paralog solely responsible for the observed in vivo phosphorylation of Lac1 and Lag1 at Ser23 and Ser24.
source: Thus, Ypk1 is the paralog solely responsible for the observed in vivo phosphorylation of Lac1 and Lag1 at Ser23 and Ser24.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that ypk1Δ but not ypk2Δ eliminates phosphorylation (Figure 3B).

claim: Under conditions that stimulate TORC2 activity, nearly all of the Lac1 and much more of the Lag1 were converted to the phosphorylated isoform.
source: Furthermore, under conditions that stimulate TORC2 activity, nearly all of the Lac1 (Figure 3B) and much more of the Lag1 (data not shown) were converted to the phosphorylated isoform indicating that TORC2 activation is relayed to ceramide synthase via Ypk1.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing increased phosphorylation of Lac1 after myriocin treatment.

claim: TORC2 inhibition markedly reduced Lac1 phosphorylation within 20 min in tor2-as cells.
source: TORC2 inhibition markedly reduced Lac1 phosphorylation within 20 min in tor2-as cells, but not in the otherwise isogenic control cells (Figure 3C), confirming that TORC2 activity is necessary for Ypk1-mediated ceramide synthase phosphorylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3C showing loss of phosphorylated Lac1 after BEZ-235 treatment in tor2-as but not TOR2 cells.

claim: Treatment with aureobasidin A markedly increased the amount of phosphorylated Lac1 and Lag1.
source: As observed for treatment with myriocin, the amount of phosphorylated Lac1 (Figure 4A) and Lag1 (data not shown) was markedly increased in response to treatment with aureobasidin A.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing increased phosphorylated Lac1 band after aureobasidin A treatment on Phos-tag gels.

claim: Within 5 min of heat shock, the amount of phosphorylated Lac1 and Lag1 increased markedly, but was back to the resting level by 30 min.
source: Within 5 min, the amount of phosphorylated Lac1 (Figure 4B) and Lag1 (data not shown) increased markedly, but was back to the resting level by 30 min.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B showing time course of Lac1 phosphorylation after heat shock with peak at 5 min.

claim: Cells co-expressing Lac1(S23A S24A) and Lag1(23A S24A) grew detectably less well when challenged with either myriocin or aureobasidin A than wild-type cells or cells co-expressing Lac1(S23E S24E) and Lag1(S23E S24E).
source: Indeed, we found that the cells co-expressing Lac1(S23A S24A) and Lag1(23A S24A) grew detectably less well when challenged with either myriocin or aureobasidin A than either otherwise isogenic wild-type cells or cells co-expressing Lac1(S23E S24E) and Lag1(S23E S24E) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C showing serial dilution growth assays on plates with myriocin or aureobasidin A.

claim: The wild-type and mutant ceramide synthase subunits were present in equivalent amounts under the conditions tested.
source: These growth differences could not be attributed to differences in the level of expression of these proteins, as immunoblot analysis demonstrated the wild-type and mutant ceramide synthase subunits were present in equivalent amounts under the conditions tested (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4D showing immunoblots of HA-Lac1 and FLAG-Lag1 with equivalent band intensities for wild-type and mutant versions.

claim: Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of Ser23 and Ser24 in Lac1 and Lag1 is functionally important for cell survival in response to the stress of limiting sphingolipid biosynthesis.
source: Thus, Ypk1-dependent phosphorylation of these sites in Lac1 and Lag1 is functionally important for cell survival in response to the stress of limiting sphingolipid biosynthesis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the growth defects of non-phosphorylatable mutants under sphingolipid stress conditions (Figure 4C).

claim: The Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) mutations generated effective phosphomimetic alleles.
source: Furthermore, the fact that the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) strain phenocopied a LAC1+ LAG1+ strain under conditions that promote phosphorylation of Lac1 and Lag1 indicates that these mutations generated effective phosphomimetic alleles.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that phosphomimetic mutants behave like wild-type under stress conditions (Figure 4C).

claim: Within <10 min of Ca2+ stimulation, there was total abrogation of phospho-Lac1 and phospho-Lag1 in wild-type cells.
source: Within <10 min, we found total abrogation of phospho-Lac1 (Figure 5A, left) and total abrogation of phospho-Lag1 (data not shown) in wild-type cells, whereas in otherwise isogenic cna1Δ cna2Δ mutants (which lack both calcineurin catalytic subunit paralogs) a substantial portion of the phosphorylated species remained (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing loss of phosphorylated Lac1 band after CaCl2 treatment in wild-type but not cna1Δ cna2Δ cells.

claim: In cna1Δ cna2Δ mutants, a substantial portion of the phosphorylated Lac1 and Lag1 species remained after Ca2+ stimulation.
source: Within <10 min, we found total abrogation of phospho-Lac1 (Figure 5A, left) and total abrogation of phospho-Lag1 (data not shown) in wild-type cells, whereas in otherwise isogenic cna1Δ cna2Δ mutants (which lack both calcineurin catalytic subunit paralogs) a substantial portion of the phosphorylated species remained (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing persistence of phosphorylated Lac1 band after CaCl2 treatment in cna1Δ cna2Δ cells.

claim: Ca2+ addition led to nearly complete Lac1 and Lag1 dephosphorylation in cells expressing constitutively-active Ypk1(D242A).
source: We found that Ca2+ addition still led to nearly complete Lac1 and Lag1 dephosphorylation in these cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B showing loss of phosphorylated Lac1 after CaCl2 treatment even in cells expressing Ypk1(D242A).

claim: Pkh1- and Pkh2-dependent phosphorylation of the activation loop in Ypk1 was not diminished in cells stimulated with Ca2+.
source: Furthermore, as judged by immunoblotting with a phospho-site specific antibody, Pkh1- and Pkh2-dependent phosphorylation of the activation loop in Ypk1 (Figure 5C) was not diminished in cells stimulated with Ca2+, confirming that there was no calcineurin-mediated decrease in the amount of active Ypk1 present.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5C showing no change in pT504 signal after CaCl2 treatment.

claim: Calcineurin dephosphorylates the sites in Lac1 and Lag1 phosphorylated by Ypk1 directly, rather than through down-regulation of Ypk1 function.
source: Therefore, it seems clear that calcineurin dephosphorylates the sites in Lac1 and Lag1 phosphorylated by Ypk1 directly, rather than through down-regulation of Ypk1 function.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observations that Ca2+ causes dephosphorylation even with constitutively active Ypk1 and does not reduce Ypk1 activation loop phosphorylation (Figures 5B, 5C).

claim: Relative to wild-type cells, the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells accumulated significantly more PHS and DHS.
source: Relative to wild-type cells, the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells accumulated significantly more PHS (Figure 6A, top left), as well as more dihydrosphingosine (DHS) (Figure 6A, top right), which is a more minor LCB in yeast (note the difference in scale of the ordinate), whereas the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) cells displayed a level of both PHS and DHS that was somewhat lower, and a similar trend was observed even for PHS-1P, an even less abundant metabolite (Figure 6A, bottom left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A showing LC-MS quantification of LCBs and LCBPs in different strains.

claim: The Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) cells displayed levels of PHS and DHS that were somewhat lower than wild-type.
source: Relative to wild-type cells, the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells accumulated significantly more PHS (Figure 6A, top left), as well as more dihydrosphingosine (DHS) (Figure 6A, top right), which is a more minor LCB in yeast (note the difference in scale of the ordinate), whereas the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) cells displayed a level of both PHS and DHS that was somewhat lower, and a similar trend was observed even for PHS-1P, an even less abundant metabolite (Figure 6A, bottom left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A showing LC-MS quantification of LCBs and LCBPs in different strains.

claim: In the absence of Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation, the rate of LCB utilization is significantly reduced.
source: Given that the ceramide synthase complex is responsible for the conversion of LCBs into ceramides, these findings indicate that, in the absence of Ypk1-mediated phosphorylation, the rate of LCB utilization is significantly reduced, consistent with the conclusion that Ypk1-dependent modification of Lac1 and Lag1 promotes ceramide synthase function.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the accumulation of LCBs in non-phosphorylatable mutants (Figure 6A).

claim: The amount of complex sphingolipids generated during pulse-labeling was reproducibly higher in the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) cells than in the wild-type controls.
source: Strikingly, the amount of complex sphingolipids generated during the pulse was reproducibly higher in the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) cells than in the wild-type controls, and Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) generated levels of complex sphingolipids lower than the wild-type controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B showing TLC analysis of 32P-labeled complex sphingolipids with quantification.

claim: Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) generated levels of complex sphingolipids lower than the wild-type controls.
source: Strikingly, the amount of complex sphingolipids generated during the pulse was reproducibly higher in the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) cells than in the wild-type controls, and Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) generated levels of complex sphingolipids lower than the wild-type controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B showing TLC analysis of 32P-labeled complex sphingolipids with quantification.

claim: Immunoblotting of exponentially-growing cultures showed no discernible difference in the steady-state level of wild-type and mutant Lac1 and Lag1.
source: Immunoblotting of exponentially-growing cultures expressing the 3xHA-tagged versions of wild-type Lac1 and Lag1 and the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) and Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) indicated no discernible difference in their steady-state level (see Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4D showing equivalent immunoblot signals for wild-type and mutant proteins.

claim: There was no difference in the efficiency of Lip1 co-immunoprecipitation between wild-type Lac1 and Lag1 and either the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) or Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) mutants.
source: Likewise, in cells co-expressing the same proteins and FLAG-tagged Lip1 (gift of Howard Riezman, Univ. of Geneva), we observed no difference in the efficiency of Lip1 co-immunoprecipitation between wild-type Lac1 and Lag1 and either the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) or Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments (data not shown).

claim: The specific activity of the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) complex was reproducibly ∼2-fold higher than either the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) mutant or the wild-type complex.
source: We found that the specific activity of the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) complex was reproducibly ∼2 higher than either the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) mutant or the wild-type complex (Figure 6C, upper panel), similar to the degree of difference in sphingolipid metabolites between these same strains that we measured by other means (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C showing in vitro ceramide synthase activity assays with immunopurified enzyme.

claim: Immunopurified ceramide synthase from wild-type cultures treated with myriocin had higher activity than ceramide synthase prepared from untreated cells.
source: Additionally, we found that immunopurified ceramide synthase from wild-type cultures treated with myriocin had higher activity than ceramide synthase prepared from untreated cells (Figure 6C, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C showing increased ceramide synthase activity after myriocin treatment in wild-type cells.

claim: The increase in ceramide synthase activity in response to myriocin treatment was not observed in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells.
source: Furthermore, this increase in ceramide synthase activity in response to myriocin treatment was not observed in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells (Figure 6C, lower panel), consistent with TORC2-Ypk1 signaling increasing ceramide synthase activity by phosphorylation at these residues.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C showing no increase in ceramide synthase activity after myriocin treatment in non-phosphorylatable mutant cells.

claim: Ypk1 phosphorylation directly increases the catalytic activity of ceramide synthase.
source: Hence, we conclude that Ypk1 phosphorylation directly increases the catalytic activity of ceramide synthase.
evidence: This conclusion is based on in vitro activity assays showing higher activity of phosphomimetic mutants (Figure 6C).

claim: Expression of Ypk1* was well tolerated by cells containing wild-type Lac1 and Lag1, but deleterious to the growth of the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) mutant cells.
source: Indeed, compared to the empty vector control, expression of Ypk1* was well tolerated by cells containing wild-type Lac1 and Lag1, but deleterious to the growth of the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) mutant cells, whether measured on agar plates (Figure 7A, top) or in liquid culture (Figure 7A, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7A showing growth assays on plates and in liquid culture.

claim: There was a reproducible and statistically significant increase in the LCBP level in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells, compared to LAC1+ LAG1+ controls.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, we found a reproducible and statistically significant increase in the LCBP level in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells, compared to LAC1+ LAG1+ controls, and a further increase in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells expressing Ypk1* (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7B showing LC-MS quantification of PHS and PHS-1-P levels in different strains.

claim: Introduction of an lcb4Δ null mutation into the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) mutant suppressed the growth inhibitory effect of Ypk1*.
source: As expected, introduction of an lcb4Δ null mutation into the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) mutant suppressed the growth inhibitory effect of Ypk1* (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7C showing growth assays of lcb4Δ strains with Ypk1* expression.

claim: The poor growth phenotype of cells lacking LCB3 was markedly exacerbated by introduction of the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) alleles.
source: Conversely, and consistent with toxicity arising from accumulation of LCBPs when Lac1 and Lag1 cannot be stimulated by Ypk1, we found that the poor growth phenotype of cells lacking the gene (LCB3) encoding the major LCBP phosphatase (Mandala et al., 1998), was markedly exacerbated by introduction of the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) alleles, but not by introduction of the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) alleles (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7D showing growth curves of lcb3Δ strains with different ceramide synthase alleles.

claim: Presence of the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) allele afforded nearly complete rescue of the slow-growth phenotype of the lcb3Δ mutation.
source: In fact, and strikingly, presence of the Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) allele afforded nearly complete rescue of the slow-growth phenotype of the lcb3Δ mutation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7D showing growth curves of lcb3Δ strains with phosphomimetic ceramide synthase alleles growing nearly as well as wild-type.

claim: Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells expressing Ypk1* exhibited a readily detectable increase in basal GFP-Atg8 processing.
source: In agreement with the poor growth arising from LCBP-evoked induction of autophagy, we found, first, that Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells expressing Ypk1* exhibited a readily detectable increase in basal GFP-Atg8 processing, comparable to that in lcb3Δ cells (but, of course, much less than that occurring when cells were treated with the starvation mimetic rapamycin) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7E showing immunoblots of GFP-Atg8 processing with quantification of free GFP.

claim: Preventing autophagy by ablating ATG1 provided substantial rescue of the growth debilitating effect of Ypk1* expression in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells.
source: Second, we found that preventing autophagy by ablating the gene ATG1, which encodes a protein kinase necessary for induction of autophagophore formation and its elongation (Papinski and Kraft, 2014), provided substantial rescue of the growth debilitating effect of Ypk1* expression in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells (Figure 7F, compare to Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7F showing growth assays of atg1Δ strains with improved growth compared to Figure 7A.

claim: Introduction of the atg1Δ mutation did not prevent the observed hyper-accumulation of LCBP in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells expressing Ypk1*.
source: This rescue was not due to an indirect effect of the absence of Atg1 on LCBP level because introduction of the atg1Δ mutation did not prevent the observed hyper-accumulation of LCBP in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells expressing Ypk1* (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7G showing LC-MS quantification of PHS-1-P levels in atg1Δ strains.

claim: Another physiologically important role of Ypk1-dependent ceramide synthase activation is to prevent hyper-accumulation of LCBPs and thereby avoid inadvertent induction of autophagy under nutrient-sufficient conditions.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that, aside from stimulating ceramide synthesis per se, another physiologically important role of Ypk1-dependent ceramide synthase activation is, at least in part, to prevent hyper-accumulation of LCBPs and thereby avoid inadvertent induction of autophagy under nutrient-sufficient conditions (Figure 8).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observations that non-phosphorylatable mutants accumulate LCBPs, show increased autophagy, and that blocking autophagy rescues growth defects (Figures 7B, 7E, 7F).

claim: 70% of the SDL hits tested served as Ypk1 substrates in vitro.
source: Gratifyingly, 12/17 (70%) of the SDL hits tested in this manner displayed readily detectable and Ypk1-specific phosphorylation (Table 1, right column).
evidence: This is stated based on the results of in vitro kinase assays with purified candidate substrates (Table 1).

claim: All known in vivo substrates of Ypk1 display robust incorporation in the in vitro kinase assay.
source: All known in vivo substrates of Ypk1 (Fpk1, Fpk2, Gpd1, Orm1 and Orm2) display robust incorporation (as judged by autoradiography) in this in vitro assay (Roelants et al., 2010, 2011; Lee et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work demonstrating in vitro phosphorylation of known substrates.

claim: Fps1 has three possible N-terminal Ypk1 sites and one C-terminal site, but only the C-terminal site is a Ypk1 target.
source: For example, Fps1 has three possible N-terminal Ypk1 sites (RPRGQT147T, RRRSRS181R and RSRATS185N) and one C-terminal site. The C-terminal site is a Ypk1 target (data not shown); however, none of the N-terminal motifs serves as a Ypk1 phospho-acceptor site (Figure 1E), most likely because each lacks a hydrophobic residue at +1.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1E showing that GST-Fps1(1-255) is not phosphorylated by Ypk1 in vitro, while the C-terminal region is (data not shown).

claim: A significant fraction (20/90) of the bioinformatically identified candidates that were tested displayed an SDL phenotype.
source: Thus, as summarized in Table 1 (column 4), a significant fraction (20/90) of the candidates identified bioinformatically that were tested in this fashion, but far from all, displayed an SDL phenotype.
evidence: This is stated based on the results of SDL screening summarized in Table 1.

claim: All known Ypk1 substrates tested (Gpd1, Fpk1, Orm1 and Orm2) displayed an SDL phenotype.
source: In this regard, it is important to note that all known Ypk1 substrates tested (Gpd1, Fpk1, Orm1 and Orm2) displayed an SDL phenotype, whereas nearly 80% of the bioinformatic hits, like GFP, did not.
evidence: This is stated based on the SDL screening results in Table 1.

claim: Over-expressed catalytically-inactive Fpk1 caused an SDL phenotype equivalent to or stronger than wild-type Fpk1.
source: Consistent with the view that the SDL phenotype could arise from the over-expressed target serving as a decoy substrate that titers a limited pool of active Ypk1 away from acting on its essential substrates, we observed that over-expressed catalytically-inactive Fpk1 caused an SDL phenotype equivalent to or stronger than wild-type Fpk1 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on SDL screening results shown in Table 1.

claim: Mammalian ceramide synthase activity increases upon heterodimerization of different catalytic subunit isoforms.
source: In this regard, it has been shown that mammalian ceramide synthase activity increases upon heterodimerization of different catalytic subunit isoforms (Laviad et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work in mammalian cells (Laviad et al., 2012).

claim: There was no difference in the state of Lac1-Lag1 association between the wild-type proteins and either the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) or Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) mutants.
source: However, as judged by co-immunoprecipitation, we found no difference in the state of Lac1-Lag1 association between the wild-type proteins and either our Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) or Lac1(S23E S24E) Lag1(S23E S24E) mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments (data not shown).

claim: Alignments of Lac1 and Lag1 homologs from Saccharomyces sensu stricto species to Ustilago maydis nearly all contain a basophilic sequence that matches the Ypk1 phospho-acceptor site consensus in their N-terminal cytosolic extensions.
source: Indeed, alignments of the primary structures of Lac1 and Lag1 homologs predicted from sequenced fungal genomes, from Saccharomyces sensu stricto species to the very distantly related Ustilago maydis, nearly all contain a basophilic sequence that matches the Ypk1 phospho-acceptor site consensus and is located, as in S. cerevisiae Lac1 and Lag1, in their N-terminal cytosolic extensions, suggests that Ypk1-related protein kinases may regulate ceramide synthase across essentially all fungal species.
evidence: This is stated based on bioinformatic analysis of fungal genome sequences.

claim: A genetic interaction between a Ypk1 homolog (YpkA) and a Lac1/Lag1-like ceramide synthase component (BarA1) has been reported in Aspergillus nidulans.
source: Consistent with this suggestion, a genetic interaction between a Ypk1 homolog (YpkA) and a Lac1/Lag1-like ceramide synthase component (BarA1) has been reported in Aspergillus nidulans (Colabardini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work in A. nidulans (Colabardini et al., 2013).

claim: Orm1 and Orm2, when phosphorylated at unique sites by protein kinase Npr1, promotes steps in the sphingolipid pathway that lead to more complex sphingolipids.
source: There is also evidence that Orm1 and Orm2, when phosphorylated at unique sites by protein kinase Npr1, promotes steps in the sphingolipid pathway that lead to more complex sphingolipids (Shimobayashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Shimobayashi et al., 2013).

claim: Npr1 is inhibited by TORC1.
source: In contrast to Ypk1, which is activated by TORC2, Npr1 is inhibited by TORC1 (MacGurn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (MacGurn et al., 2011).

claim: TORC1 negatively regulates the autophagy-inducing protein kinase Atg1-Atg13 complex.
source: Under the same condition, autophagy is induced because, like Npr1, TORC1 also negatively regulates the autophagy-inducing protein kinase Atg1-Atg13 complex (Alers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Alers et al., 2014).

claim: Sch9 promotes transcriptional repression of genes (YDC1 and YPC1) that encode ceramidases and inhibits a phosphosphingolipid phospholipase C (Isc1) that hydrolyzes complex sphingolipids.
source: This is likely because Sch9 promotes transcriptional repression of genes (YDC1 and YPC1) that encode ceramidases and inhibits a phosphosphingolipid phospholipase C (Isc1) that hydrolyzes complex sphingolipids (Swinnen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Swinnen et al., 2014).

claim: In cells lacking the calcineurin regulatory subunit (Cnb1), there was an increase in C26-containing ceramides.
source: Subsequently, it was observed that, in cells lacking the regulatory subunit (Cnb1), there was an increase in C26-containing ceramides, suggesting that calcineurin somehow antagonizes TORC2-dependent signaling (Aronova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Aronova et al., 2008).

claim: Calcineurin recognizes substrates via a docking motif (PxIxIT or variants thereof), typically also accompanied quite a distance upstream by a secondary docking site (LxVP).
source: Calcineurin recognizes substrates via a docking motif (PxIxIT or variants thereof), typically also accompanied quite a distance upstream by a secondary docking site (LxVP) (Roy and Cyert, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Roy and Cyert, 2009) on calcineurin substrate recognition.

claim: The more hydrophobic variant PVIVIT is much more potent in recruiting calcineurin when it is used to replace the native 'PxIxIT' sequences in either the transcription factor Crz1 (PIISIQ) or the endocytic adaptor Aly1 (PILKIN).
source: However, these sites can be quite degenerate; for example, the more hydrophobic variant PVIVIT is much more potent in recruiting calcineurin when it is used to replace the native 'PxIxIT' sequences in either the transcription factor Crz1 (PIISIQ) (Roy et al., 2007) or the endocytic adaptor Aly1 (PILKIN) (O'Donnell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Roy et al., 2007; O'Donnell et al., 2013).

claim: In both Lac1 and Lag1, there is a similar hydrophobic sequence (355PIVFVL360) located at the identical position in both proteins.
source: In both Lac1 and Lag1, there is a similar hydrophobic sequence located at the identical position in both proteins (355PIVFVL360).
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis of Lac1 and Lag1.

claim: Heat shock leads to a transient increase in sphingolipid production.
source: Consistent with that response, it has been shown previously that heat shock leads to a transient increase in sphingolipid production and that sphingolipid production is important for heat shock survival (Jenkins et al., 1997; Cowart et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Jenkins et al., 1997; Cowart et al., 2003).

claim: Sphingolipid production is important for heat shock survival.
source: Consistent with that response, it has been shown previously that heat shock leads to a transient increase in sphingolipid production and that sphingolipid production is important for heat shock survival (Jenkins et al., 1997; Cowart et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Jenkins et al., 1997; Cowart et al., 2003).

claim: Measurement of pathway intermediates and mathematical modeling suggested that a sharp spike of increased ceramide synthase activity may occur after heat shock.
source: Moreover, measurement of pathway intermediates and mathematical modeling also suggested that a sharp spike of increased ceramide synthase activity may occur after heat shock (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Chen et al., 2013).

claim: Accumulation of LCBPs has been shown to be toxic to yeast cell growth.
source: Given that accumulation of LCBPs has been shown to be toxic to yeast cell growth (Kim et al., 2000), we reasoned that the most likely metabolic perturbation responsible for the observed decrease in growth in the Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells expressing Ypk1* was the build-up of LCBs and derived LCBPs.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Kim et al., 2000).

claim: Aberrant increases in LCBP level impede growth by triggering autophagy even under nutrient-rich conditions.
source: Finally, it has been reported that aberrant increases in LCBP level impede growth by triggering autophagy even under nutrient-rich conditions (Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Zimmermann et al., 2013).

claim: An elo3 mutation, which prevents efficient formation of C26-CoA, was synthetically lethal with lcb3Δ.
source: Consistent with the toxicity of LCBPs when LCB utilization by ceramide synthase is inefficient, an elo3 mutation, which prevents efficient formation of C26-CoA (an acyl chain found in yeast ceramides), was synthetically lethal with lcb3Δ (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Kobayashi and Nagiec, 2003).

claim: Atg1 encodes a protein kinase necessary for induction of autophagophore formation and its elongation.
source: Second, we found that preventing autophagy by ablating the gene ATG1, which encodes a protein kinase necessary for induction of autophagophore formation and its elongation (Papinski and Kraft, 2014), provided substantial rescue of the growth debilitating effect of Ypk1* expression in Lac1(S23A S24A) Lag1(S23A S24A) cells (Figure 7F, compare to Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Papinski and Kraft, 2014).

claim: A previous study found a consistent decrease in ceramide synthase activity in microsomal fractions isolated from cells in which TORC2 had been inactivated.
source: Consistent with our findings, a previous study found a consistent decrease in ceramide synthase activity in microsomal fractions isolated from cells in which TORC2 had been inactivated (and thus Ypk1 activity was presumably reduced) (Aronova et al., 2008), although indirect effects of the loss of TORC2 function on ceramide synthase activity could not be ruled out.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Aronova et al., 2008).

claim: Membrane stress caused by inhibition of sphingolipid synthesis or membrane stretch causes Slm1 and Slm2 to relocalize from eisosomes to a separate PM region that contains TORC2.
source: It has been reported that membrane stress caused by inhibition of sphingolipid synthesis or membrane stretch (induced by hypotonic shock) causes two PH domain-containing proteins (Slm1 and Slm2) to relocalize from eisosomes to a separate PM region that contains TORC2 and leads to increased TORC2 activation of Ypk1 and Ypk2 (Berchtold et al., 2012), purportedly because Slm1 and Slm2 recruit Ypk1 and Ypk2 to TORC2 (Niles et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Berchtold et al., 2012; Niles et al., 2012).

claim: Avo1 is the subunit of the TORC2 complex primarily responsible for substrate recognition of Ypk1 and its orthologs.
source: However, other evidence indicates that Avo1 (ortholog in other organisms is Sin1) is the subunit of the TORC2 complex primarily responsible for substrate recognition of Ypk1 and its orthologs, including association of S. cerevisiae Ypk2 with Avo1 (Liao and Chen, 2012), Gad8 with Sin1 in fission yeast (Ikeda et al., 2008; Kataoka et al., 2014), and SGK1 with mSin1 in mammalian cells (Jacinto et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple previous studies in different organisms (Liao and Chen, 2012; Ikeda et al., 2008; Kataoka et al., 2014; Jacinto et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013).

claim: Ypk1 is activated at a basal level by phosphorylation of a Thr in the activation loop by the eisosome-associated protein kinase Pkh1 (and its paralog Pkh2).
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Ypk1 (and Ypk2) are activated at a basal level by phosphorylation of a Thr in the activation loop by the eisosome-associated protein kinase Pkh1 (and its paralog Pkh2) (Casamayor et al., 1999; Roelants et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Casamayor et al., 1999; Roelants et al., 2002).

claim: The ortholog responsible for activation loop phosphorylation of Ypk1 in mammalian cells is PDK1.
source: The ortholog responsible for this reaction in mammalian cells is PDK1 (Mora et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Mora et al., 2004).

claim: Basal Ypk1 activity from Pkh1/Pkh2 phosphorylation is not sufficient for Ypk1 to permit survival when cells are challenged with certain membrane perturbants.
source: However, this level of activity is not sufficient for Ypk1 to permit survival when cells are challenged with certain membrane perturbants (Roelants et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work (Roelants et al., 2004).

claim: Ypk1 and Ypk2 are two members of the AGC kinase family and orthologs of mammalian SGK1.
source: Ypk1 (and Ypk2) are two members of the AGC kinase family (Pearce et al., 2010) and orthologs of mammalian SGK1 (Casamayor et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Pearce et al., 2010; Casamayor et al., 1999).

claim: Dynamic changes in the function of TORC2 and Ypk1 are important for cell survival in response to membrane stress.
source: We (Roelants et al., 2011) and others (Berchtold et al., 2012; Niles and Powers, 2012) have shown that dynamic changes in the function of Target of Rapamycin (TOR) Complex 2 (TORC2) and in a downstream protein kinase that it stimulates, Ypk1 (and its paralog Ypk2), are important for cell survival in response to membrane stress.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work (Roelants et al., 2011; Berchtold et al., 2012; Niles and Powers, 2012).

claim: Levels and distributions of lipids are important for PM processes including solute transport, endocytosis, and receptor function and signal transduction.
source: The levels and distributions of lipids are clearly important for PM processes—from solute transport (Divito and Amara, 2009), to endocytosis (Platta and Stenmark, 2011), to receptor function and signal transduction (Groves and Kuriyan, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on different PM processes (Divito and Amara, 2009; Platta and Stenmark, 2011; Groves and Kuriyan, 2010).
